title: Harmonic extends its Aristotle theorem prover to C and Verilog verification
subtitle: The $1.45 billion math-focused AI startup said on October 27 that its Lean 4 reasoning agent can now check C software and Verilog chip designs — the first commercial push to move a math-grade AI prover into the hardware-verification stack.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Harmonic — the mathematical-reasoning startup backed by Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev and co-founded by Tudor Achim — announced on October 27 that its Aristotle theorem-proving agent can now be used to formally verify C software and Verilog chip designs. Aristotle was designed as a Lean 4 proof agent and reached gold-medal performance at the 2025 International Math Olympiad on a formal evaluation track. The extension to Verilog and C moves the system from pure-math benchmarks into the actual tooling that chip and systems companies use to prove that a design matches its specification.

Formal verification is already a routine, if expensive, part of serious hardware work — proving by machine-checked math that a circuit cannot violate a safety property, no matter the inputs. The bottleneck has never been the solvers; it is the engineer-hours needed to write the specifications and guide the proofs. Harmonic's pitch is that an agent that can autonomously produce thousand-line proofs in Lean 4 is the same shape of tool a verification engineer wants pointed at a Verilog module. The company is hiring formal-verification engineers and research engineers in formal methods, and a Harmonic engineer gave a Cambridge talk earlier this year titled 'Automatically Formally Verified Hardware using Aristotle,' which previewed the direction.

The context around the announcement is less flattering. Harmonic made news earlier in 2026 for an Erdős-problem result that Terence Tao and other mathematicians argued was not actually novel, and Kevin Weil of OpenAI deleted a congratulatory post after the pushback. The company is still pre-revenue, offered Aristotle through a free API, and raised a $120 million Series C with Nvidia participation at a $1.45 billion valuation. Moving into hardware verification is both a sharper commercial fit — chip and defense customers pay for verification engineer-hours in a way the pure-math community does not — and a cleaner falsification target, because the output either passes an existing commercial model-checker's checks or it does not.

A note for learners: this is the quietest and arguably the most important front in applied AI right now. The industries that will adopt AI theorem provers first are the ones where a bug is catastrophic and the economics of verification are already brutal — avionics, high-reliability chips, cryptography, parts of medical devices. If you want a career path that is likely to be AI-amplified rather than AI-replaced, learn one proof assistant (Lean, Rocq, or Isabelle), one hardware description language (Verilog or SystemVerilog), and read the public verification standards (ARP 4754, ISO 26262, Common Criteria). People fluent in both the formal methods and the regulated domain will be rare for years.
